classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a linear derivative graph to infer the original function's shape and the location of its maximum.

content.prompt: Describe the graph of $y=f(x)$ if the graph shown below is $y=f'(x)$.

spec.description: Unscaled Cartesian axes with a descending straight derivative line, arrowheads at both ends, positive y-intercept and positive x-intercept. No ticks, grid or numerical labels.
spec.mathematics: A straight line of negative slope represents f'(x). Its single zero lies to the right of the y-axis. Drawing coordinates are schematic and do not supply numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: The derivative graph is permanently visible; the description of f(x) is answer-only.

answer.short: A concave down parabola with its vertex to the right of the $y$-axis.
answer.worked: The derivative is a decreasing straight line, so $f(x)$ is a concave down parabola. Before the positive $x$-intercept, $f'(x)>0$, so $f$ increases. After it, $f'(x)<0$, so $f$ decreases. Therefore the vertex is a maximum to the right of the $y$-axis.
